rationale: A wins slightly because it does more than name plausible pegs; it tells the founder which proof would make each angle survive a reporter's follow-up. Its best line, "Educators Say Duolingo Is Gamified Fluff. Its Users Are Spending Nine Minutes on AI Conversations," creates real tension while admitting nine minutes is not learning. B is disciplined, but "Duolingo says engagement is at an all-time high" misstates the supplied fact: DAU hit a new high, engagement did not. That factual wobble gets a pitch killed before the smarter work underneath gets read.
gaps_in_A: "Duolingo's 40% User Growth and Profitability Are Not a Coincidence" implies causality the update does not prove. Growth plus profitability is interesting; "not a coincidence" is punditry unless Duolingo supplies conversion, margin, or cohort evidence.
"Why Duolingo Made Chess Free and AI Tutoring Expensive" overstates two facts: the update says paid Max video conversations, not "AI tutoring," and it gives no price basis for "expensive."

"whether Duolingo is pivoting from language app to AI learning platform" is a useful thesis, but thin. One free chess course and one AI language feature need an exec quote or roadmap before this becomes more than a raised eyebrow.
"The comparison to human tutoring is immediate" is a smart market lens, but not grounded in the update. It needs tutor-platform data or tutor reactions fast, or it becomes a straw competitor angle.
gaps_in_B: "Duolingo says engagement is at an all-time high" is the bad kind of tidy. The update says DAU grew 40% to a new high and beta video sessions averaged 9 minutes; it does not say overall engagement is at an all-time high.
"Record DAU, profitable, two new product bets in the same quarter" invents the quarter frame. The facts give a same-announcement peg, not a quarter-level narrative.
"ahead of earnings" is an imported markets peg with no support in the update. Publicly traded does not automatically mean there is an earnings-timing story today.

"the \"what gets gated\" question showing up across consumer subscription products" may be a real trend, but B does not ask for enough proof: Max price, subscriber count, conversion data, and comparable companies all belong there.
